concepts.title: Why Sociology is a Science: Method and Objectivity
concepts.definition: Sociology earns the name of science less from laboratories than from method: systematic observation, comparison and evidence open to checking by others. Its object -- human beings who think and react -- makes controlled experiment hard, so objectivity means disciplined self-awareness about one's own biases rather than a value-free machine.
concepts.key_idea: Science is a discipline of evidence, not a place -- sociology studies people systematically while admitting the observer's presence.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy105.txt lines 15-130 (introduction, sociology as a science, objectivity, difficulties of studying human behaviour, method as disciplined procedure)
question_patterns: is sociology a science explain with reasons
in class 11 doing sociology: why is objectivity difficult in social research
what makes a study systematic and scientific
can a sociologist be completely value free
distinguish the subject matter of natural and social sciences
how do sociologists check their own biases

solution_steps.explain: Science means claims justified by evidence gathered systematically and open to others' scrutiny.
People interpret, react and change; laboratory control is often impossible or unethical.
The researcher documents procedures, invites replication and reflects on bias -- objectivity as disciplined practice.

worked_examples.q: Sociology earns the name of science mainly through what: method or laboratories?

concepts.title: Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary
concepts.definition: Social researchers draw on primary data collected first-hand from the field -- interviews, observation, questionnaires -- and secondary data already recorded by others -- censuses, official reports, newspapers, parish or panchayat records. Each source has strengths and blind spots, so studies often mix them.
concepts.key_idea: First-hand fieldwork or second-hand records -- know what each source can and cannot tell you.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy105.txt lines 130-240 (sources of data, primary and secondary sources, census and survey material, documents and records, advantages and limitations)
question_patterns: distinguish primary data from secondary data with examples
in class 11 doing sociology: what are the merits and limitations of census data
why might official records mislead a researcher
when would a sociologist prefer documents to interviews
list the sources of secondary data in social research
how can primary and secondary sources be combined in one study

solution_steps.explain: Data you generate yourself is primary; data generated by others for their purposes is secondary.
Primary data fits your question but costs time; secondary data is cheap and broad but shaped by others' categories and errors.
Combining sources lets one check the other, guarding against the bias of any single record.

worked_examples.q: Interviews and observation collect which data: primary or secondary?

concepts.title: The Survey, Sampling and the Questionnaire
concepts.definition: A survey asks standardised questions of many respondents to map patterns across a population. Since interviewing everyone is impossible, researchers sample -- selecting a smaller set chosen so that it represents the whole -- and questionnaires or schedules collect the answers for quantitative analysis.
concepts.key_idea: Ask the same questions of a well-chosen few and read the many -- that is the survey's craft.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy105.txt lines 240-360 (survey method, sampling, population and sample, questionnaire and schedule, advantages and limitations of surveys)
question_patterns: what is a survey and when is it the appropriate method
in class 11 doing sociology: explain the idea of sampling in social research
distinguish a questionnaire from an interview schedule
why must a sample be representative
what are the limitations of the survey method
design a small survey to study internet use among students

solution_steps.explain: State exactly whom the study is about -- all students, all farmers of a district -- the group to which findings should apply.
Select a manageable subset by a rule that gives everyone a known chance of inclusion, so the sample mirrors the population.
A fixed questionnaire or schedule asks everyone the same items, allowing answers to be counted and compared.

worked_examples.q: Selecting a smaller set chosen to represent the whole is called what?

concepts.title: Interview, Observation and Fieldwork in Anthropological Tradition
concepts.definition: Qualitative methods probe meaning: interviews range from free conversation to guided discussions, letting respondents speak in their own terms; participant observation -- living among the people studied, as in classic village and slum studies -- records social life from inside. Fieldwork of this kind trades scale for depth and context.
concepts.key_idea: Live among, listen to, and record -- qualitative methods capture what numbers leave out: meaning.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy105.txt lines 360-470 (interview method, participant observation, fieldwork tradition in sociology and anthropology, strengths and weaknesses of qualitative methods)
question_patterns: describe participant observation as a method of sociology
in class 11 doing sociology: what are the merits and demerits of the interview method
how does fieldwork build understanding of a community
compare the survey with participant observation
what does the researcher risk losing and gaining by living in the field
when is an unstructured interview better than a questionnaire

solution_steps.explain: Participant observation places the researcher in the daily life of the group, watching practices as they happen.
Interviews -- structured to unstructured -- record meanings and reasons in people's own vocabulary.
Field notes, extended residence and reflexive checking yield depth and context, at the cost of small numbers and slow generalisation.

worked_examples.q: Living among the people studied is called what kind of observation?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A researcher wants to know how students of a 2000-strong college use libraries but can interview only 200. Walk through the design choices she must make.

solution_template.explain: The population is all 2000 students of the college -- the group findings must describe.
She selects 200 students so that course, year and gender proportions match the college, making the sample representative.
A short questionnaire with closed questions lets her count patterns; findings extend to the college only if sampling was fair.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A sociologist studies a fishing village by living there for a year, helping with nets and recording daily life. Identify the method and weigh its strengths and weaknesses.

solution_template.explain: Living in and joining the community's work is participant observation in a fieldwork tradition.
It reveals routines, meanings and informal rules invisible to surveys -- the insider's view.
One village cannot represent all fishing communities, and closeness may bias what the researcher sees; both limits must be stated.
